description: We are a driven team combining computer engineering, hardware simulation, and full-stack web development. We're looking for enthusiastic teammates skilled in hardware design, coding, design, or data analysis to build an impactful space solution together
summary:
AstroPatch is an integrated hardware and software system for autonomous health monitoring of astronauts on long-duration missions. We designed a wearable microneedle patch and a web-based mission dashboard (astropatch-app.vercel.app).
Hardware. We designed the full electrical schematic in KiCad 10, organized into functional blocks: Li-Ion charging and power regulation (MCP73831, MCP1700), an environmental sensor (BME280), an electrochemical analog front end for the microneedle electrodes (INA128), a mechanical-strain and skin-contact channel (LMC6482), NTC/PTC thermistor compensation, and an ESP32-WROOM-32 for acquisition and BLE/Wi-Fi telemetry.
Software. The web app shows tissue and ambient pressure, interstitial-fluid biochemistry (glucose, lactate, electrolytes, cortisol), vitals, and device status. An action engine turns this data into clear guidance. The demo runs on simulated telemetry in several scenarios: normal operation, EVA, decompression/fatigue alert, and offline deep-space mode.
Challenge and impact. Crews far from Earth must detect physiological changes themselves. AstroPatch gives them continuous, interpretable indicators and actionable status without relying on ground support.
AI disclosure. AI was used only to generate images for the presentation and the website. The circuit design and the software are our own work.
details:
AstroPatch is a wearable monitoring system with two parts: a microneedle patch and a web-based mission dashboard.

On the hardware side, the patch measures several signals:

  • Interstitial-fluid biochemistry. Microneedle electrodes feed an INA128 instrumentation amplifier, which extracts weak electrochemical signals and rejects common-mode noise.
  • Mechanical state. An LMC6482 rail-to-rail op-amp conditions strain and skin-contact signals from the microneedle array.
  • Skin temperature. NTC and PTC thermistors in resistor dividers allow software temperature compensation of the biosensor readings.
  • Ambient and suit pressure. A BME280 reports pressure, humidity and air temperature.

An ESP32-WROOM-32 digitizes these signals and transmits them over BLE/Wi-Fi. Power comes from a Li-Ion cell with an MCP73831 charge controller (4.2 V termination) and an MCP1700 low-dropout regulator.

The dashboard (astropatch-app.vercel.app) presents:

  • a pressure and decompression monitor;
  • microneedle biochemistry (glucose, lactate, Na⁺/K⁺, cortisol);
  • vitals and device status;
  • an action engine that turns the data into clear guidance, such as EVA clearance or a critical alert.

It also shows the Earth communication delay and supports four scenarios: Normal, EVA, Critical Alert (decompression/fatigue) and Deep Space Offline mode. The demo currently runs on simulated telemetry.

Benefits and intended impact

On long missions, crews must spot physiological changes in themselves, often with communication delays. AstroPatch aims to give them continuous, interpretable health indicators and a clear status (Normal / Attention / Action) without constant ground support. Combining pressure, biochemistry and temperature in one patch supports early detection of decompression risk, fatigue and stress.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Hardware: ESP32-WROOM-32, BME280, INA128, LMC6482, MCP73831, MCP1700, NTC/PTC thermistors, Li-Ion cell.
  • PCB design: KiCad 10 (hierarchical, color-zoned schematic with ERC-clean power flags).
  • Web app: Next.js, deployed on Vercel.
  • Presentation: Canva.
  • AI: used only to generate images for the presentation and website. The circuit design and software are our own work.

Creativity

  • Integrated sensing. One compact device covers environmental, mechanical, biochemical and thermal channels.
  • Temperature compensation. Dual thermistors correct the biosensor readings in software.
  • Interpretation first. The dashboard presents decisions and status levels rather than raw data alone.
  • Offline-first. A deep-space mode reflects communication delays and outages.

Factors our team considered

  • Size, weight and power: low-dropout regulation and a compact single-cell design.
  • Signal integrity: instrumentation amplification for microvolt-level electrochemical signals.
  • Safety and reliability: clear alert states and a graceful offline mode.
  • Usability: simple status levels for astronauts working under stress.
  • Next steps: board prototype, sensor calibration and connecting real patch data to the app.
